threads_text: Binance says about $6.3 billion in crypto was stolen, the biggest crypto theft on record, and blockchain trackers point at North Korea. It reportedly started with one engineer's compromised laptop. Would you still keep your crypto on an exchange?
caption:
Binance says about $6.3 billion in crypto was stolen from its hot wallets, the largest crypto theft on record.
It may have started with one engineer's compromised laptop. TRM Labs and Chainalysis point to North Korea's TraderTraitor group.
Binance says it will cover all losses, and close to $3 billion has been frozen.

Would you still keep your crypto on an exchange?

Follow @neurafeed.ai for daily AI news.

slides.headline: North Korea is suspected in a *$6.3 billion* Binance heist, the biggest crypto theft ever

slides.heading: The *biggest heist* on record

paras: Binance's first finding: a DevOps engineer's compromised laptop let the attacker reach a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawals.

slides.heading: Billions *frozen* fast

paragraphs.text: Binance, which holds more assets than any other crypto exchange according to CoinMarketCap data cited by Al Jazeera, said about $6.3 billion in crypto assets was stolen in a security incident it confirmed late on October 29, 2026, Eastern time, according to AFP and Al Jazeera. The theft is the largest crypto heist on record, roughly four times the $1.5 billion taken from the exchange Bybit in February 2025.

Blockchain analytics firm TRM Labs counted about $6.36 billion leaving Binance wallets on ten blockchains, while Chainalysis put the figure at about $6.4 billion, Help Net Security reported. ABC News in Australia reported that 30 to 40 tokens were affected, including Bitcoin, Ethereum and the stablecoins USDT and USDC, all moved out of internet-connected hot wallets.

Binance said its initial investigation pointed to a compromised laptop belonging to a DevOps engineer. According to the company, that access allowed the attacker to reach a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions. A Binance spokesperson said the company had found no evidence of a wallet private key leak.

TRM Labs offered a more detailed early reading. On Ethereum, the attackers took control of a Binance hot wallet using 50 authorizations that had been signed in advance, which TRM initially believed were phished. Wallets on other chains, which use different key types and signing schemes, also produced valid signatures for the attackers within about half an hour. TRM said that pattern points to a compromise of the exchange's hot wallet signing infrastructure.

TRM Labs assessed with high confidence that the attack was carried out by TraderTraitor, a North Korean hacking unit that the FBI named in the Bybit theft and that investigators have linked to the Lazarus Group. Chainalysis chief executive Jonathan Levin said the hack was likely done by the same group because of links to a previous hack. Ari Redbord, TRM's global head of policy, told Al Jazeera that money stolen by North Korea at this scale funds weapons proliferation. Binance has not named a culprit and said it is working with law enforcement partners to identify those responsible.
Binance founder Changpeng Zhao, who no longer runs the exchange but remains a major shareholder, wrote on X that it did look like a hack and said he expected user funds to be covered.

Binance said it will cover all losses from its SAFU emergency fund and company funds and that user funds are safe. It suspended deposits and withdrawals while it ran security checks; a later update said deposits were operating normally, while withdrawals remained paused, with resumption expected within 48 hours. The company also promised a technical post-mortem and an updated proof of reserves.

Stablecoin issuers moved quickly. Tether chief executive Paolo Ardoino said the company froze more than 1.567 billion USDT, and Circle chief executive Jeremy Allaire said Circle froze more than 800 million USDC in coordination with law enforcement. Ripple, World Liberty Financial and Arbitrum's Security Council also froze funds. Binance put the total frozen at close to $3 billion, and Help Net Security reported that the attackers still held more than 420,000 ETH and 18,270 BTC, worth about $2.4 billion.

Bitcoin fell about 5 percent after the theft and dropped below $77,000, Al Jazeera reported. CoinDesk reported total liquidations of about $1.5 billion across crypto markets, and Standard Chartered's Geoffrey Kendrick said he expected the price decline to continue until frozen assets are released and more details emerge.

The scale of the theft matters as much as the method. A single compromised work laptop appears to have opened a path to signing systems across many blockchains, which suggests that the weakest point at a major exchange may be ordinary employee devices rather than the wallets themselves. The fast response from stablecoin issuers also shows how much recovery now depends on a few companies that can freeze tokens on request, a power that only covers part of the stolen assets.

The next marker is Binance's technical post-mortem and whether withdrawals reopen within the 48 hours the company promised, along with how much of the roughly $2.4 billion in unfrozen ETH and BTC moves through bridges and brokers.
